\chapter{Naming the Whole --- Family, Nickname, Relative, Partner, Baby}
\label{ch:familia-y-pareja}
\hlchaptermodality{309}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a family, a partner, a relative and a baby in Spanish, and I can say what somebody is called by nickname as well as by name and surname.}

Complete ES-C309-bebe: gather the whole household into one word, add the third kind of name, and close on the youngest person in the room.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la familia]{la familia --- the household, servants included}

\label{lesson:ES-C309-familia}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la familia} --- \textquotedblleft{}the family.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{familia} did not mean what you think. It meant the whole household --- the people, the servants, the property, everything under one roof and one authority. The root is \textbf{famulus}, \textquotedblleft{}a servant.\textquotedblright{} Blood was not the point; belonging to the house was.

English took the word and narrowed it to relatives. But the older sense survives in \emph{familiar}: to be familiar with something is to be at home with it, and a \emph{familiar} --- in the old sense --- was a spirit attached to a household.

The stress lands on the \textbf{i}: \emph{fa-MI-lia}. The \textbf{-lia} at the end is one syllable, not two.

You now have a word that gathers up everything in the chapter before it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One word that holds all fifteen of the people you have named.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la familia}
  \item \emph{la familia y la gente}
  \item \emph{el apellido de la familia}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who was in a Latin \emph{familia}? (Everyone in the household, servants included.) What is a \emph{famulus}? (A servant.) What does \emph{familiar} really mean? (At home with something.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el apodo]{el apodo --- the name somebody reckoned for you}

\label{lesson:ES-C309-apodo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el apodo} --- \textquotedblleft{}the nickname.\textquotedblright{}

It comes from \emph{apodar}, \textquotedblleft{}to nickname,\textquotedblright{} and behind that sits Latin \textbf{putare}. \emph{Putare} first meant to \textbf{prune} a tree --- to cut it back into shape. From trimming a tree it moved to trimming a problem, and so to \emph{reckon}, \emph{judge}, \emph{consider}.

English is full of the pruned version. To \emph{compute} is to reckon together. To \emph{dispute} is to reckon apart. Your \emph{reputation} is what people reckon about you over and over. And to \emph{amputate} is the oldest sense back again, cutting off.

So an \emph{apodo} is a name somebody reckoned up for you --- a judgement, trimmed to one word. Which is exactly what a nickname is.

Set it beside what you already have. Your \emph{nombre} was given to you, your \emph{apellido} was inherited, and your \emph{apodo} was decided by other people.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third kind of name --- and the only one you do not choose.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el apodo}
  \item \emph{el nombre y el apodo}
  \item \emph{el apodo del niño}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{putare} mean first? (To prune a tree.) How did it get to \emph{compute}? (Pruning to reckoning.) Which of your three names do other people decide? (The \emph{apodo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pariente]{el pariente --- not the parent}

\label{lesson:ES-C309-pariente}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pariente} --- \textquotedblleft{}the relative.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{parere} meant to bring forth, to give birth. The one giving birth was a \textbf{parens}, and that is English \emph{parent}. It is also \emph{postpartum}, \textquotedblleft{}after the bringing forth,\textquotedblright{} and it is hiding inside \emph{viper} --- \emph{vivipara}, the creature that bears its young alive.

Now the warning, and it matters more than the etymology. \emph{Pariente} does \textbf{not} mean parent. It means any relative at all --- the cousin, the aunt, the grandmother. This is your second false friend, and a sharper one than \emph{chico}, because here the words really are related and the meanings still drifted apart.

One more caution, because the resemblance is very convincing. English \emph{apparent} looks like it belongs here and does not: that is Latin \emph{apparēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to appear,\textquotedblright{} a different verb that happens to look almost identical. Two Latin verbs, nearly the same shape, unrelated in sense.

Related words can mislead you exactly because they are related.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that means more than it looks like --- and a caution about trusting resemblance.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pariente}
  \item \emph{el pariente y la familia}
  \item \emph{un pariente, señor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{parere} mean? (To bring forth.) Does \emph{pariente} mean parent? (No --- any relative.) Is \emph{apparent} from the same verb? (No --- a different Latin verb that looks alike.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pareja]{la pareja --- two of equal weight}

\label{lesson:ES-C309-pareja}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la pareja} --- \textquotedblleft{}the couple,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}the partner.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{par} meant equal. \emph{Pareja} is \textbf{paricula}, \textquotedblleft{}a little equal\textquotedblright{} --- two things matched in weight.

English is thick with it. A \emph{pair} is two equals. \emph{Par} in golf is the equal score. Your \emph{peers} are your equals. \emph{Parity} is the state of being equal. To \emph{compare} is to set things side by side as equals.

The best one is \emph{umpire}. It was \textbf{noumpere} in Middle English --- \emph{non par}, \textquotedblleft{}not equal,\textquotedblright{} the third person who is not on either side and can therefore decide. English then misheard \emph{a noumpere} as \emph{an oumpere}, and the n moved house. The word for the one who is not equal is built out of the word for equal.

So \emph{pareja} says something specific about a couple: not one and one, but two of matching weight.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Nineteen words, and a root that runs from golf to refereeing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la pareja}
  \item \emph{la pareja y la familia}
  \item \emph{mi pareja, encantado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{par} mean? (Equal.) What is an \emph{umpire} literally? (\emph{Non par} --- not equal, so able to decide.) What does \emph{pareja} say about a couple? (Two of matching weight.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el bebé]{el bebé --- the sound, not the word}

\label{lesson:ES-C309-bebe}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el bebé} --- \textquotedblleft{}the baby.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish took this from French \textbf{bébé}, and French did not take it from anywhere. It is echoic: the \emph{b}-noise infants actually make, repeated. English \emph{baby}, \emph{babe} and \emph{babble} are the same act of listening, done separately.

This closes the loop the chapter opened. \emph{Niño} was babble too. The oldest and most careful words here --- \emph{esposo} from a Roman legal pledge, \emph{gente} from a Roman clan register --- are the formal ones. The words for the smallest people are noises.

Two points of form. The written accent on the final \textbf{é} pulls the stress to the last syllable: \emph{be-BÉ}. Without it Spanish would stress the first. And \emph{el bebé} stays masculine whoever the baby is; the word has a gender, the child need not match it.

You began this stretch able to give your own name. You can now name everyone else in the room.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twenty people named --- and the last of them arrived as a sound.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el bebé}
  \item \emph{el bebé y la niña}
  \item \emph{el nombre del bebé, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did \emph{bebé} come from? (French, and before that nowhere --- it is babble.) What does the accent do? (Pulls the stress to the last syllable.) Is \emph{bebé} masculine for a girl too? (Yes --- the word has a gender, the child need not match.)
\end{tcolorbox}
